notes:
## Blocks end where their reading ends

- In Write mode with text to speech on, every block now ends where its reading ends, as in Frazier. To make a block longer or shorter, change its speed, from its menu or with **[** and **]**.
- A block’s edges can no longer be dragged, and OUT shows where the reading ends. Dragging a block, or changing its IN, moves the whole block. Splitting and merging keep each end at its reading.
- Blocks opened from a file keep their timing until you edit them.
- The settings **Set the end of new blocks from the reading** and **Change a block’s reading speed when you resize it** are gone, since this always happens now.
- In Transcribe mode, and with text to speech off, edges drag as before.

## Natural speeds

- **Fit speeds to timings** never slows a reading below −15%, so a short line in a long block still sounds natural, with silence after it.

## Try voices before switching

- Picking a voice in the text to speech settings, from the list or your favourites, now only tries it out. **Test** reads with it, and nothing else changes, so you can go through voices without being asked about the timings each time.
- When you’ve found the one you want, click **Apply**, next to Test. Every block then reads with it, and you’re asked about the timings once. Close Settings without Apply and the voice stays as it was.

## Your own test line

- A new **Test text** box under the voice holds what Test reads. It starts with the sample description; type any line to hear it in each voice. It’s remembered for next time.

## Fixes

- Every block now fits its reading as you edit it. Blocks marked with H, drawn on the timeline or opened from a file keep their length, and their reading speeds up or slows down to fill it. A block with a speed you picked keeps that speed, and its end moves to where the reading finishes. Before, these blocks kept both their length and their speed, so a longer line ran past the end of its block.

## Fixes

- After **Shift+V** or **Update all timings** set a block’s end from its reading, the end now keeps following the reading as you edit the text, as a new block’s does. Before, it stayed where it was, so a longer line, or a Google reading that came out longer than its estimate, left the block too short, marked ⚠, with its reading running past the end. This also applies when you open a script and choose to change the ends to match the readings.

## Fixes

- Resizing a block now settles on a reading speed that fills it in a reading or two. Before, with Kokoro voices especially, the speed could wander for a few seconds, through speeds whose readings ran past the block’s end, and stop somewhere slightly off.
- Resizing a block whose speed you picked by hand now says that it keeps that speed, and how to have the reading fill the block instead.

## A voice for each block

- The block editor has a new **Voice** menu next to the speed. Leave it on **Same as Settings** to use the voice chosen in Settings, or pick another voice for just that block, for example a different voice for subtitles or a second narrator.
- Blocks with their own voice show its name in the list. Playing, fitting, Make all readings and exported description tracks all use each block’s own voice, and a track can mix Piper, Kokoro and Google voices.
- Block voices are saved in projects and WebVTT exports. Frazier `.adc` files bring their per-block voices with them.
- If a block’s voice isn’t available, for example a Kokoro voice in the web version, it reads with the voice in Settings until it is.

## Replace all voices

- When blocks have voices of their own, the text to speech settings say which, with a **Replace all voices** button that sets every block back to the voice chosen there. Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes it.

## Steadier fitting

- Fitting a block’s speed now settles on the reading that fills the block best without running over. Before, it could stop on a speed that came out slightly short or a little long, especially with Kokoro voices.

## Make all readings

- A new **Make all readings** button in the text to speech settings reads every block now, at its own speed, without changing any timings. Each block then plays straight away and its length is exact.
- The readings are kept in your browser, so they're still ready after a reload or the next time you open the project, and they work offline.
- It runs in the background, with its progress and a Stop button in the bottom bar. Blocks already read are skipped.
- It needs a Piper, Kokoro or Google voice. With a Google voice, it reads with Google every block that hasn't been read yet, which uses up your free characters.

## Readings kept across reloads

- Piper and Kokoro readings are now kept in your browser, as Google's already were. After you reload or reopen Scribecue, blocks already read keep their ● dot and exact length, and play straight away, even offline.
- Up to 250 MB of readings are kept. When that fills up, Piper and Kokoro readings go first, since they're free to make again, then the ones used longest ago. Settings, under Storage, shows them as Saved readings and can clear them.

## Readings on time while playing

- While playing, Scribecue now makes the next blocks' readings ahead of the playhead. Before, a reading was only made as its block began, so Kokoro voices, which take a second or more, started late and ran past the end of their block. Exported description tracks were never affected.

## Updates in the web version

- If you opened Scribecue shortly before an update came out, the update could keep some of the previous version's files, so a fix it brought didn't reach you until the next one. Updates now always fetch every file fresh.
- If Piper voices were still missing after 0.48.2, this brings them back. Your downloaded voices were kept, so there's nothing to download again.

## Piper voices in the web version

- Piper voices are back in the web version. Since 0.48.0, Scribecue couldn't see them: the Natural voices section was hidden, and voices you'd downloaded were missing from the voice list, so blocks were read with a browser voice instead. Your downloaded voices were kept, so they're there again without downloading them.
- The note about Kokoro voices, under Natural voices, shows again too.

## Kokoro voices

- The web version's text to speech settings now mention Kokoro voices, under Natural voices. They sound even more like a person reading and are free, but need Scribecue running on your computer with Docker, since they're too big and slow to run well in a browser. A link shows how to add them.

## Kokoro voices

- Running Scribecue with Docker, you can now add Kokoro, a free, open-source voice model whose voices sound closer to a person reading than Piper's. It runs in its own container, so your script stays on your computer and it works offline.
- It has 41 voices in US and UK English, Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian and Brazilian Portuguese, in their own Kokoro group in the voice menu.
- As with Piper, lengths are exact and you can export a description track. Each reading takes a second or two.
- To add it, put `kokoro` in `COMPOSE_PROFILES` in your `.env` file, such as `COMPOSE_PROFILES=piper,kokoro`, then run `docker compose up -d --build`. INSTALL.md has the details.
- Kokoro isn't in the web version yet.

## When a voice isn't available

- If a project's voice isn't available, such as a Google voice in a browser without your key, or a Piper voice while Piper isn't running, Scribecue now says so, and which voice is reading instead. The text to speech settings say what to do about it.
- Saving a project keeps its own voice. Before, the voice standing in for it was saved instead, so the project lost its voice.

## Google Cloud voices

- While you type in a block, Scribecue no longer reads it with Google each time you pause. The length shown is an estimate until you finish editing, with Enter or Esc or by moving to another block, and then the block is read once. Rewriting a line several times no longer uses up characters for every draft.
- Piper and browser voices still update the length as you type, since they cost nothing.

## Readings in the block list

- A dot (●) after a block's duration in the list means its reading has been made with the chosen voice, at its speed and the base speed, so its length is exact.
- With a Google Cloud voice, the dot means the reading is kept in your browser: it plays straight away and isn't sent to Google again. Hover over it to see which.
- Screen readers say "reading ready" for those blocks.

## Changing the voice or base speed

- When Scribecue asks what to do with the timings, you can now **go back** to the voice or base speed you had, and nothing changes.
- With a Google Cloud voice, Scribecue now warns that changing the ends, fitting the speeds or updating all timings reads every block with Google again. That uses up your free characters, and may cost money once they run out. Lines already read at the same voice and speed aren't sent again.

## Base speed

- The **Speed** menu in the text to speech settings is gone: the **Base speed** slider now sets the speed of the whole project, as in Frazier. Blocks without a speed of their own read at normal speed.
- If you had chosen a speed in that menu, it's now your base speed, so fast (+15%) becomes 115%.
- The setup wizard asks for a base speed, and the setting for what happens to timings is now called **When the voice or base speed changes**.

## Base speed

- **Settings**, under **Text to speech**, has a **Base speed** slider from 50% to 150%, as in Frazier. Every reading is made this much faster or slower, on top of its own speed, so you can nudge a whole project without changing any block's speed. Double-click it to go back to 100%.
- The base speed is saved with each project, and a Frazier `.adc` script's base speed now comes with it, so its blocks keep their own speeds by name.

## When the voice or speed changes

- Changing the voice, the speed or the base speed changes how long every reading takes. Scribecue now asks whether to change the blocks' ends to match the new readings, never running into the next block, or leave the timings as they are. Tick **Always do this** to stop it asking, and change your choice under **When the voice or speed changes**. Changing the ends can be undone with Ctrl/Cmd+Z.

## Frazier scripts

- **Open** (Ctrl/Cmd+O) now opens Frazier's `.adc` scripts, and you can drop them on the window too. Each block keeps its timings to the millisecond.
- Block speeds come across as the matching Scribecue speed, on top of the project's base speed.
- Pronunciations marked in Frazier become **sounds like** words, so the text stays as written and text to speech says it your way.

## Favourite voices

- In **Settings**, under **Text to speech**, click ☆ beside the voice list to pin the current voice to your favourites. Click it again to unpin it.
- Your favourites appear as buttons under the voice list, so you can switch between them in one click, and at the top of the voice list itself.
- If a favourite isn't available, for example because Piper is off, its button is dashed, and clicking it removes it.

## Google Cloud voices

- Readings from Google are now kept in your browser, so each line is only sent to Google, and counted against your allowance, once. It's read again only if you change its text, speed or voice.
- Reopening a project, playing it back or exporting the description track uses the kept readings, so lengths are exact straight away, and lines already read play offline.
- **Settings**, under **Storage**, shows how many readings are kept and can clear them. Up to 250 MB are kept, the ones used longest ago going first.

## Google Cloud voices

- Text to speech can now use Google Cloud's **Standard** voices, with your own Google Cloud key. Add it in **Settings**, under **Text to speech**, and the voices in your languages appear in the voice list. Like Piper voices, they give exact lengths straight away and can be exported as a description track. Each reading sends the block's text to Google.
- The key stays in your browser and is only sent to Google, along with Scribecue's address and nothing else, so you can restrict the key to Scribecue's website.
- A new guide, **Google voices**, covers setting up the key and making sure you're never billed. It's in **Guides**, in the shortcuts overlay.

## Opening a script

- When you open a script, its timings are worked out in the background, whether you chose what to do or Scribecue used your usual choice. A progress bar with **Stop** shows at the bottom while it runs, and you can carry on working with the script meanwhile.

## Mix

- A new slider under the video, between **Video** and **TTS**, sets how loud the readings are against the video's sound. Double-click it to put it back in the middle. Scribecue remembers where you left it.

## Block list

- The selected block, or the one playing, moves to the top of the list, so you can see the blocks coming up below it. A block you click stays where it is.

## Time remaining

- Click the total length, next to the clock under the video, to show the time left instead. It counts down as the video plays. Click it again to go back, and Scribecue remembers which you chose.

## Reading it yourself

- In Write mode, while you hold **H** to time your own read, the block's text stays on the video until you let go, even once the playhead passes its old end.

## Tour and setup

- The tour has caught up with Settings: one step shows you Settings and what to set up first for your mode, and a new step covers what's on under the video, such as REPLAY.
- Setup's text to speech step now asks about Replay too, as the transcribing step does.

## Fixes

- **Alt+Shift+V** and **Alt+Shift+H** open their settings in either mode, as Settings does.
- Messages that pointed to the old text to speech panel, to TTS under the video or to the version number now point to Settings.
- The tour only says setup comes next when it does.

## Settings

- **Settings**, at the top (**Alt+Shift+S**), puts everything you set up in one window, so the screen has less on it while you work. Its sections are **General**, **Transcribing**, **Text to speech**, **AI help**, **Keyboard shortcuts** and **Storage**.
- The **Setup** button at the top has moved into Settings, under **General**, as **Run setup again**, next to **Take the tour**. The storage button in the bottom right is in Settings too. **offline** still shows there while you're offline.
- AI help's provider, key and model are set in Settings, under **AI help**, along with your TMDB key for looking up the cast. The drawer's **Settings** button opens it.
- **REPLAY**, **STT** and **TTS** under the video show only while they're on, and clicking one, or the reaction offset, opens its section. The usual keys, such as **Alt+Shift+V** and **Alt+Shift+H**, open their sections too.

## Replay

- After you edit a block and press **Esc** or **Enter**, the playhead goes back to the block's start, so you can hear it again. If the video was playing, it carries on from there. It works in both modes.
- Replay is on unless you turn it off: **Shift+L**, or in Settings under **General**.

## Find and replace

- **Replace…**, next to the block search, or **Alt+Shift+F**, changes text in every block at once, such as a character's name. **Match case** and **Whole words only** are there if you need them (Tom, but not Tomorrow). **Find next** steps through the blocks it's in, and one Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes **Replace all**.

## Sounds like, for every block

- In Sounds like, tick **Use them in every block with these words** to add your pronunciations to every other block that has those words too, in one step.

## Projects remember their video

- In Chrome and Edge, opening a project, or Scribecue again, now reopens its video too. After a restart the browser asks first: click **Reopen**, with the video's name, where the video goes.

## Fix

- Transcribed blocks now start with a capital letter. Whisper sometimes wrote "they speed off." when a block started partway through a sentence.

## Look up the cast for your project notes

- In AI help's **Notes**, **Look up the cast** fills in the character names for you. Paste the programme's IMDb link, or type its title, and click **Look up**. An episode's own link adds its guest cast too.
- The characters and their actors come from [TMDB](https://www.themoviedb.org/), a free film and TV database, and are added below your notes, ready to add how to tell people apart.
- It uses your own free TMDB key. The first time, Scribecue asks for it, with a link to get one. Only the link or title you look up goes to TMDB.

## Fix

- **Keep it safe**, in the storage window, now shows the browser's answer right there. Before, it seemed to do nothing, because the answer appeared behind the window.
- Chrome and Edge decide for themselves whether to keep Scribecue's storage, so they may say no. If they do, the window says so and offers **Ask again**. Saving your work as a project keeps it safe either way.

## Install the Docker version as an app

- **Install app** in the bottom right now shows in the Docker version too, whenever Chrome or Edge can install Scribecue. It gets its own window and icon, like the web version. It still opens from Docker, so Docker needs to be running.

## Punch in when you time your own read

- Holding **H** in Write mode now works like punching in on a recording: it plays from wherever the playhead is in the selected block.
- **Need a breath?** Let go at a comfortable point, then hold H again to carry on from there. The pause doesn't count, so the block is as long as your reading.
- **Fluffed a word?** Step back with ← → to just before it and hold H to redo the rest.
- **To start over,** press **G** to go to the block's start, then hold H. Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes one part at a time.

## Storage, in the Docker version

- The Docker version runs from your computer, so it has nothing to get ready for working offline. Its button in the bottom right now says **storage**, and opens a **Storage** window about what's kept in this browser: whether it's kept safe, the space used, what needs a connection, and **Remove all data**.
- The web version's **Offline and storage** window is unchanged.

## Time your own read with H

- In Write mode, select a block and **hold H**. It plays from the block's start while you read the line aloud; let go when you finish, and the block ends there. Hold H again to retake, and Ctrl/Cmd+Z goes back a take.
- It works with text to speech off or on, and live reading stays quiet while you hold H.
- The reaction offset (**H −200ms** under the video) now applies in Write mode too, and **Shift+H** changes it in both modes.

## Sounds Like, from a selection

- Select a word in a block's text and a **Sounds Like** button pops up under it. Click it and Sounds like opens with the word already filled in, so all that's left is typing how it should sound.
- It shows **Sounds Like ✓** for a word that already has a pronunciation. Alt+Shift+P still works too.

## Screen readers

- Scribecue's messages, such as "Block #3 marked", are now read out by screen readers, with key symbols said as words.
- The block list is a list a screen reader can move through: each block is read with its number, start, length and text, and the selected one is marked.
- The buttons and indicators under the video say what they do, and whether they're on, and the clock says it copies the timecode.
- A reading too long for its block now says "too long", and gets a ⚠ in the list, not only red.
- Faint grey text is a little lighter, so it's easier to read.

## Also

- **Transcribe** and **Write** are now a sliding switch at the top left. Click either side, or the side that's on, to switch.

## Remove all data

- The offline window is now **Offline and storage**, opened from the bottom right, in the Docker version too. It ends with **Remove all data**, which clears everything Scribecue keeps in this browser: unsaved blocks, settings and shortcuts, AI keys, downloaded Piper voices and Whisper, and its offline copy.
- It warns you first, says how many unsaved blocks would be lost, and offers to save the project. Your project files, and anything in Docker, stay as they are. Afterwards Scribecue opens as if for the first time.

## Fix

- Browsers built on the same engine as Chrome, such as Brave, Opera, Vivaldi and Arc, no longer get the notice about features that may not work, unless something really is missing. Scribecue now checks what your browser can do, rather than going by its name, and only lists what it lacks.

## Working offline

- **offline ready** in the bottom right opens a checklist of what this browser has for working without a connection: Scribecue itself, the guides, your Piper voices and Whisper, and whether the browser will keep them. Anything missing has a button to get it.
- While you're offline, the bottom right says **offline**. AI help says when an online provider can't be reached, and points to Ollama, which works offline. Online voices are greyed out.
- Scribecue now asks the browser to keep its storage, so it's less likely to be cleared when space runs low.

## Guides inside Scribecue

- The README and the transcribing, AI and install guides now open inside Scribecue, with their screenshots, and work offline. **Guides** in the shortcuts overlay (press ?) opens them, and links to them anywhere in Scribecue open there too.

## Phones, tablets and old browsers

- On a phone or tablet, Scribecue now says it needs a computer, rather than opening an editor that can't be used there.
- Browsers from before 2022, too old to run Scribecue, now say so instead of showing a blank page.

## Autosave

- Autosave is now always on wherever it works. The status next to the project name only shows what it's doing; click it when it says **autosave paused** or **autosave failed** to carry on. If you'd turned autosave off, it's back on.
- Autosave only runs in browsers that can save straight back to a file, which are Chrome and Edge. In Firefox and Safari, the notice when Scribecue opens now says autosave isn't available there.

## Fix

- The autosave status now sits right after the project and video names at the top, where it's easy to find, instead of over by the buttons on the right.

## Autosave

- Once a project has a file, Scribecue now saves your changes to it as you work, a couple of seconds after you stop. **autosaved** next to the project name says it's done.
- After a reload, the browser asks before Scribecue may save to the file again, so the status says **autosave paused**. Click it, or press Ctrl/Cmd+S, and it carries on. Opening a project asks straight away.
- Click **autosaved** to turn autosave off, and **autosave off** to turn it back on. The file always has your latest changes, so save a copy with Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+S before a big change if you might want the old version.
- Autosave needs Chrome or Edge. In other browsers, the reminder to save still helps.

## Speech to text

- **Spelling:** Whisper writes American spelling, and the speech to text panel can now change it to British and Canadian spelling as the text arrives: colour, grey, centre, travelled, catalogue and the like. It starts on whichever suits your browser's language.
- The panel links to the new [transcribing guide](https://github.com/kyle95wm/Scribecue/blob/main/TRANSCRIBING.md), which covers everything about transcribing, from choosing the description track to fixing what Whisper gets wrong.

## A reminder to save

- Until you save a project, your work is only kept in the browser. After 20 minutes of unsaved work, a note now asks you to save it. **Later** asks again in half an hour.

## Fix

- **Install app** in the bottom right now only shows when your browser can install Scribecue. It used to show everywhere, including when Scribecue was already installed and in the Docker version, where clicking it did nothing.

## Firefox

- In Firefox, the notice when Scribecue opens now also says what doesn't work well there: a file's description track can stutter or cut out, and speech to text can interrupt the video's sound. If you turned the notice off, it shows once more with the new list.
- The speech to text panel says so too. Both work best in Chrome or Edge.

## Fixes

- With speech to text on, marking a few blocks could stop the video's sound altogether in Firefox. Each block's audio is now read without holding on to the browser's audio decoders.
- A file's description track, when it plays alongside the video, no longer stutters or cuts out briefly in Firefox. It stays in step with fewer, gentler adjustments.
- The Whisper container leaves half your processor for the browser, so playback stays smooth while a block is transcribed. It's just as fast.

## Speech to text, for transcribing

- In Transcribe mode, **Whisper** can type each line for you. You still time every block by holding H; when you let go, Whisper listens to the block's audio and fills in what the narrator said, ready to check. If you start typing first, it leaves the block to you.
- Click **STT** under the video, or press Alt+Shift+H, to set it up. In the web version, Whisper is a one-time 166 MB download into your browser, and then it works offline. With Docker, add the new Whisper container, which is more accurate (see [INSTALL.md](https://github.com/kyle95wm/Scribecue/blob/main/INSTALL.md#speech-to-text-whisper)).
- **Transcribe empty blocks** fills in every block with no text yet, in one go. Ctrl/Cmd+Z undoes it.
- Alt+Shift+T transcribes the selected block again, such as after you change its timing.
- It all runs on your computer: the audio is never uploaded. Whisper understands English, and it hears everything in a block, so choose the description track with T if your file has one.

## Only models that work, in AI help

- **Load models** in AI help's settings now only lists models that can look at your frames and write a description. Ones that couldn't help, such as models that only handle text, make pictures, speak, or work in slow batches, are left out, for every provider.
- For Ollama, models you've downloaded that can't see images aren't listed. If none can, the settings say which one to download.

## The loop, when you need it

- The loop to work in now shows after setup, for the mode you picked, instead of inside the guided tour. The first time you switch to the other mode, its loop shows too.
- **Show the loop** in the shortcuts overlay (press ?) brings it back any time.

## Also

- Setup's text to speech step now has **Don't read notes in [square brackets]**.
- AI help has a new guide, [AI.md](https://github.com/kyle95wm/Scribecue/blob/main/AI.md): connecting each provider, which models to use, including Ollama models for each size of computer, and getting the best descriptions. AI help's settings link to it.
- Drafts with Ollama keep more room for frames and the script around the block, so long requests aren't cut short.

## What's new, after every update

- When Scribecue updates, a window like this one now lists everything that changed since the version you were on, newest first.
- Click the version number in the bottom right to see this release's notes again.

## Piper voices in setup

- In the web version, setup now offers to download a natural-sounding Piper voice, with the voices in your language first and the download size. It downloads in the background when you finish, and it's chosen once it's ready.
- Piper is now marked as recommended, in setup and the text to speech panel: its voices sound natural, give exact reading lengths, and can be exported as a description track.

## The tour comes first, and shows you the loop

- On a first visit, the guided tour now comes first, and the setup follows when it ends, whether you finish it or skip it with Esc. Setup at the top still runs just the setup, and the tour is in the shortcuts overlay (press ?).
- The tour now ends with the loop to work in for your mode: finding a gap, writing and hearing a description in Write mode, or playing, marking and typing each line in Transcribe mode. It uses your own keys if you've changed them.
- Exports are now described as "to hand off".

## Change your keyboard shortcuts

- Press **?** and click **Change shortcuts** to give any editor action the keys you like. Click **Add** and press the keys; if they already belong to another action, Scribecue asks before moving them. Click a key to take it off, and **Reset** puts an action back.
- **Export** saves your shortcuts as a file and **Import** loads one, so a team can share a layout.
- The shortcuts overlay and the player buttons' tooltips show the keys you're using.
- Keys with Ctrl/Cmd, keys used while typing, and ? / [ ] + − Esc stay as they are.

## A guided tour

- A one-minute tour now lights up each part of Scribecue in turn and explains it: the two modes, the video and timeline, the block editor and list, text to speech, AI help, projects and exports, privacy, and where the shortcuts are.
- Setup offers it at the end, and **Take the tour** in the shortcuts overlay (press ?) shows it again. Use → and ← to step through, and Esc to stop.

## Also new

- A small GitHub mark in the bottom right opens Scribecue's page on GitHub: the source, releases and a place to report problems.
- Setting Scribecue up yourself with Docker now has its own guide, [INSTALL.md](https://github.com/kyle95wm/Scribecue/blob/main/INSTALL.md), so the README is just about using it.

## A tidier header

- **Open** is now one button for everything: a project, a script (SRT or VTT), or a video or audio file, and you can pick several at once, such as a project and its video. Each opens as the right thing. Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+O still opens only video or audio.
- **Export** is now a small menu: the script as SRT (Ctrl/Cmd+E), the script as WebVTT (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+E), and in Write mode the description track (WAV).
- Every keyboard shortcut is unchanged.

## Clear the blocks, keep the video

- **New** now asks how you want to start again. **Clear the blocks** removes every block and keeps the video, the project file and your notes, ready to write from scratch on the same video. **New project** clears everything and closes the video, as before.
- Either way, Ctrl/Cmd+Z brings the blocks back.

Tip: to swap in a different script, just open it with Ctrl/Cmd+O. That replaces the blocks and keeps the video.

## The web version updates without asking

- No more "reload" prompt for every release. A new version is used as you open Scribecue, before you've started anything.
- If one arrives while you're working, nothing interrupts you: the version number in the bottom right shows **update ready**. Click it to update then, or it's used the next time you open Scribecue.
- Your blocks, notes and settings are kept either way.

This release itself still arrives with one last reload prompt, because the previous version is the one that spots it. From now on, updates happen on their own.

## Headroom in the exported description track

- The exported description track is no longer at full scale. Every reading now peaks at −8 dBFS, so blocks are evenly matched and there's headroom for processing and mastering.
- Readings that run into the next block overlap in the file, but never take it past −6 dBFS.

## Fix: exporting a long description track in the web version

- In the web version, exporting a description track, or other long jobs such as Fit speeds to timings, with a Piper voice could stop with "Couldn't export the description track: Aborted()." This came in with 0.22.0 and happened after about 80 blocks. Long exports now finish.

The Docker version wasn't affected. Running it? Update as usual: `git pull`, then `docker compose up -d --build`.

## A more realistic voice test

## New: Piper voices, exact timings and description track export

Scribecue can now use [Piper](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl), an open-source speech engine with natural-sounding voices, running in a second container next to the editor. Its voices run on your computer and work offline, so your script never leaves it. Piper is optional: Scribecue works as before without it.

With a Piper voice, in Write mode:

- **Lengths are exact straight away.** A block's reading time is exact as soon as it has text, and **Update all timings** uses the real readings in a second or two, with no silent read-through.
- **Each line always takes the same time,** so the timing you see is the timing you get, between sessions and in the export.
- **Export description track** saves every block's reading as one WAV file, each starting at its block's start time and as long as the video, ready to mix with the programme. It tells you if any readings overlap.

Four English voices are included: Lessac and Ryan (US), and Alba and Alan (UK). You can choose others from the Piper voice list.

### Setting it up

Create a file called `.env` in the Scribecue folder containing `COMPOSE_PROFILES=piper`, then run `docker compose up -d --build`. The first build downloads Piper and its voices, about 1 GB. After that the Piper container has no internet access, and only Scribecue's own server can reach it. See the README for details.

In the Scribecue folder, run `git pull` and then `docker compose up -d --build`, and reload the page. Your text blocks and settings are kept. To add Piper at the same time, create the `.env` file first.
